1.title: AI approaches and scope
1.objective: Compare rule-based, predictive and generative systems using their inputs and outputs.
1.idea: AI is a broad field of systems performing tasks associated with intelligence. Machine learning fits behavior from data, and deep learning uses multilayer neural networks within machine learning. Rules can be useful without learning, while a generative model produces candidate content rather than guaranteeing its truth. Historical milestones and research labels describe approaches; AGI and ASI are proposed capabilities, not evidence that a product has them.
1.example: A hand-written rule sends invoices over 100 units for review; a fitted classifier predicts fraud; a language model drafts an explanation. The first need not learn, and the draft still needs evidence checking.
1.practice: Classify an invoice rule, a fitted spam filter and a text-drafting assistant; write one input, output and failure condition for each.

questions.question: Is every AI system trained?
questions.answer: No. Symbolic rule systems can use explicitly authored rules.

questions.question: Does generating an answer establish that it is supported?
questions.answer: No. Generation and verification are separate tasks.

1.mistake: Calling every automated rule a learned model hides the distinction between authored rules and fitting from data.

1.title: Product lifecycle and evidence
1.objective: Diagnose two risks in a proposed AI feature before choosing a system.
1.idea: A useful product starts with a bounded user need and a non-AI baseline. Data collection, development, evaluation and monitoring form a lifecycle rather than a one-time model choice. Benefits and risks depend on who uses the output, what action follows and whether failures can be detected.
1.example: A support tool drafts a reply from approved documents. A wrong refund promise harms customers, so the design requires source review and human approval before sending.
1.practice: For a support draft and an inventory forecast, name the affected user, a simple baseline, a failure and a measurable review check.

questions.question: What comes before selecting a model?
questions.answer: A defined task, constraints and a baseline against which the model can be evaluated.

questions.question: Does an offline benchmark establish deployment safety?
questions.answer: No. Deployment introduces users, changing inputs and consequences outside that benchmark.

1.mistake: A model demonstration is not a complete product evaluation; check the surrounding workflow and consequences.

2.title: Execution and computer resources
2.objective: Explain a saved program from file storage to process execution.
2.idea: Storage retains a program file; a process is a running instance with memory and operating-system resources. Threads share a process address space, so concurrent access needs care. CPUs, GPUs and other accelerators have different execution designs; a GPU does not automatically make every workload faster. Binary representation explains why text and numeric values require an encoding.
2.example: Saving hello.py changes a file. Running python hello.py starts an interpreter process; its output is displayed in the terminal. Closing the process does not delete the saved file.
2.practice: Save a greeting file, run it from its folder, then run from another folder using its absolute path; record the working directory for each run.

questions.question: Is RAM the same as persistent storage?
questions.answer: No. Process memory is working state; the saved file persists separately.

questions.question: Will an added GPU necessarily accelerate printing a greeting?
questions.answer: No. Tiny serial work may gain nothing and accelerator overhead can dominate.

2.mistake: A terminal is an interface for commands, not the program file or the Python language itself.

2.title: HTTP and structured data contracts
2.objective: Diagnose a malformed request against a small HTTP and JSON contract.
2.idea: Networking delivers messages between endpoints. HTTP supplies methods, status codes and headers, while JSON represents structured data in the message body. HTTPS protects transport when correctly configured; it does not validate business meaning or authorize an action.
2.example: Contract: POST /ask accepts an object with a string question. {"question":"hours"} satisfies those fields; ["hours"] is valid JSON but violates the object contract.
2.practice: Write three request bodies for /ask: valid object, wrong field type and valid JSON with the wrong root type; predict acceptance or rejection.

questions.question: Is valid JSON sufficient for a valid request?
questions.answer: No. The shape and field types must meet the application contract.

questions.question: Does HTTPS authorize a requested action?
questions.answer: No. Authentication and authorization still need application controls.

2.mistake: A 400 response is an application rejection; a connection failure means no usable HTTP response arrived.

2.title: Algorithms and data structures
2.objective: Compare a list scan and a hash lookup for the same search task.
2.idea: An algorithm is a procedure; a data structure organizes the values it uses. A list scan may inspect every item, while a hash table typically offers expected constant-time key lookup under suitable hashing assumptions. Big O describes growth, not an exact stopwatch result. Recursion needs a stopping case, and tree or graph traversal also needs a way to avoid unwanted revisits.
2.example: For [4,7,9], scanning for 9 compares three entries. A dictionary {4:"a",7:"b",9:"c"} can retrieve the value by key without an explicit Python scan.
2.practice: Trace linear search for present and absent targets in a five-item list; contrast it with a dictionary lookup and explain the space tradeoff.

questions.question: Does O(1) mean one CPU instruction?
questions.answer: No. It means the modeled operation count is bounded independently of input size.

questions.question: What prevents unbounded recursive calls?
questions.answer: A reachable base case and progress toward it.

2.mistake: Expected hash-table performance is not a universal worst-case guarantee.

2.title: Storage, versioning and debugging
2.objective: Diagnose a regression using a test and a versioned change.
2.idea: A database stores records with a query interface; SQL expresses operations on relational tables. Version control records changes to project files, not the truth of program outputs. Tests compare observed behavior with explicit expectations, while modular boundaries let a failure be isolated.
2.example: A function returns 3 for input (1,2), and a test expects 3. Changing the function to multiplication makes that test fail with 2, so the regression is observable.
2.practice: Create a small add function and assertion, deliberately introduce multiplication in a separate copy, then record the failing and corrected results; optionally commit the corrected file.

questions.question: Does committing a file prove it works?
questions.answer: No. A commit records content; executed checks provide separate evidence.

questions.question: Why separate calculation from printing?
questions.answer: The calculation can then be tested without coupling the test to terminal formatting.

2.mistake: A passing test establishes its checked case, not all possible inputs or the absence of bugs.

3.title: Setup, syntax and environments
3.objective: Implement a repeatable Python setup with one importable module.
3.idea: Python executes statements from a saved file, and indentation groups suites such as function bodies. Modules provide names that other files can import. A virtual environment isolates installed Python packages but is not an operating-system security sandbox.
3.example: Save greet.py with def greet(name): return "Hello, " + name. A second file importing greet and printing greet("Ada") should display Hello, Ada.
3.practice: Create greet.py and a caller, run the caller from the project folder, and record python --version plus the command used to create a virtual environment.

questions.question: Does a virtual environment isolate all file access?
questions.answer: No. It separates Python package environments, not operating-system permissions.

questions.question: Why can importing a module run statements?
questions.answer: Top-level module statements execute when the module is first loaded in that interpreter session.

3.mistake: Installing a package globally does not establish that it exists in the selected virtual environment.

3.title: Values and collections
3.objective: Compute a deduplicated frequency table from a short list.
3.idea: A list retains sequence order and duplicates; a set represents distinct hashable elements. A dictionary maps keys to values, while tuples provide immutable sequences. Strings are immutable text values, and operators act according to operand types. Comprehensions construct collections but should remain readable.
3.example: For words=["red","blue","red"], set(words) contains red and blue, and {w:words.count(w) for w in set(words)} maps red to 2 and blue to 1; set display order is not a promised result.
3.practice: Count normalized words in [" Red ","blue","RED"] using a dictionary; explain which information the set alone would discard.

questions.question: Does a set preserve duplicate counts?
questions.answer: No. Distinct membership loses multiplicity.

questions.question: Can a list be used as an ordinary dictionary key?
questions.answer: No. Lists are mutable and unhashable.

3.mistake: A shallow copy of a collection does not recursively copy nested mutable objects.

3.title: Control flow and reusable functions
3.objective: Implement a function that filters and transforms values with explicit boundaries.
3.idea: Conditionals select a branch, and loops repeat work over values. A function returns a result and creates a local scope; type hints describe intended types but do not enforce them by themselves. Generators yield values lazily, and decorators wrap or transform callable behavior. Lambda expressions provide small anonymous functions, not a separate execution model.
3.example: def positives(xs): return [x*2 for x in xs if x>0] gives [4,6] for [-1,0,2,3]. Zero is excluded because the condition is strictly greater than zero.
3.practice: Implement doubled_nonnegative and test [-1,0,2], an empty list and [3]; predict each result before running it.

questions.question: Does a type annotation reject a wrong type automatically?
questions.answer: No. Runtime validation must be implemented separately when required.

questions.question: What changes when >0 becomes >=0?
questions.answer: Zero is included and contributes a zero result.

3.mistake: Printing a result is not returning it; callers receive None when a function falls through without a return value.

3.title: Files, errors, objects and tests
3.objective: Diagnose an invalid record without hiding the failure.
3.idea: File handling must distinguish text decoding, parsing and business validation. Exceptions signal failures that callers may handle, but a broad catch can conceal defects. Objects combine state with behavior, while tests and logs serve different purposes: assertions check expectations and logs record events.
3.example: int("12") returns 12; int("twelve") raises ValueError. Handling that specific conversion failure can report an invalid age without pretending the age is zero.
3.practice: Write parse_age with a stated policy for empty, numeric and nonnumeric strings; test every branch and preserve missing as unknown rather than zero.

questions.question: Should every exception become a success message?
questions.answer: No. Report or propagate failures according to the contract.

questions.question: Does a printed log line prove an assertion passed?
questions.answer: No. An assertion must execute and its outcome must be observed.

3.mistake: Catching Exception around an entire program can hide programming errors unrelated to the invalid input.

3.title: Libraries, clients and performance
3.objective: Compare a dependency-free transformation with a proposed library-based workflow.
3.idea: NumPy supports array operations, pandas tabular work and plotting libraries visual summaries. Notebooks retain execution state, so a clean restart helps reveal hidden dependencies. Asynchronous clients overlap waiting; they do not automatically accelerate CPU-bound Python work. External packages and hosted notebook environments are optional tools with installation or connectivity requirements.
3.example: A pure Python sum([1,2,3]) returns 6. Re-running a notebook cell that appends 3 to a persistent list can change its result, showing why cell order matters.
3.practice: Process three numeric rows with the standard library, then write a dependency list for an optional pandas/chart version; explain how to reproduce it from a clean session.

questions.question: Does async make every calculation parallel?
questions.answer: No. It primarily supports cooperative concurrency, often while waiting for I/O.

questions.question: What is a notebook reproducibility check?
questions.answer: Restart the kernel and run all cells in order using documented dependencies.

3.mistake: Timing one tiny run without controlling setup and repeated measurements is weak evidence of a performance improvement.

4.title: Vectors and similarity
4.objective: Compute dot product, norms and cosine similarity for two vectors.
4.idea: The dot product sums coordinate products. A Euclidean norm is the square root of the sum of squared coordinates, and cosine divides the dot product by both norms. Scaling a nonzero vector by a positive constant preserves its direction and cosine, while a zero vector requires explicit handling.
4.example: For a=(1,0), b=(1,1): dot=1, ||a||=1, ||b||=sqrt(2), cosine=1/sqrt(2)≈0.707. For 2b, both numerator and the b norm double, so cosine is unchanged.
4.practice: Calculate dot product, norms and cosine for a=(0,1), b=(1,1), then for a and 2b; explain why matrix shape and coordinate order must agree.

questions.question: What is the cosine for a=(0,1),b=(1,1)?
questions.answer: 1/sqrt(2), approximately 0.707.

questions.question: Can a zero vector use the same denominator?
questions.answer: No. The denominator is zero.

4.mistake: A larger dot product may reflect magnitude rather than a closer direction.

4.title: Derivatives and gradients
4.objective: Compute one gradient-descent step for a quadratic loss.
4.idea: A derivative measures local change, and a gradient collects partial derivatives for multiple parameters. The chain rule connects derivatives through composed operations; automatic differentiation applies such rules to a computation. Gradient descent subtracts learning rate times gradient, so the rate controls the step size.
4.example: For L(w)=(w−3)^2, L'(w)=2(w−3). At w=0 with rate 0.1, w_new=0.6 and new loss=5.76 instead of 9; rate 2 gives w_new=12 and loss=81.
4.practice: Repeat the quadratic step from w=1 using rates 0.1 and 2; record the new parameter and loss for each.

questions.question: What is the derivative at w=1?
What happens at rate 0.1 from w=1?

4.mistake: A larger learning rate can overshoot and increase loss rather than accelerate convergence.

4.title: Conditional probability
4.objective: Compute precision and recall using their different conditioning events.
4.idea: Conditional probability changes the population being considered. Precision conditions on a positive prediction, while recall conditions on a true positive class. Joint distributions, independence assumptions and sampling models determine which probability calculations are justified; one high rate cannot substitute for another.
4.example: Of 100 examples, 10 have a condition. Flagging 8 of those and 9 of the other 90 gives TP=8,FP=9,FN=2; precision=8/17≈47% and recall=8/10=80%.
4.practice: Keep TP=8 and FN=2 but reduce FP from 9 to 4; recompute precision and recall and explain which changed.

questions.question: What is the revised precision?
questions.answer: 8/(8+4)=2/3, approximately 66.7%.

questions.question: What is the revised recall?
questions.answer: 8/(8+2)=80%, unchanged.

4.mistake: High recall alone does not make a positive result reliable; inspect the false-positive denominator.

4.title: Samples and uncertainty
4.objective: Compare the sensitivity of two equal observed sample rates.
4.idea: A sample rate summarizes observed successes, not certainty about a population. Sampling design and representativeness determine whether an interval or hypothesis test is meaningful. Equal rates from different sample sizes can have different uncertainty, while correlation and statistical significance do not establish causation.
4.example: Reference expectation: 4/5 and 80/100 both equal 0.8. Changing one existing failure to a success while keeping each sample size fixed gives 5/5=1.0 and 81/100=0.81: increases of 20 and 1 percentage points. Appending a new successful trial instead changes both numerator and denominator, giving 5/6≈0.833333 and 81/101≈0.801980: increases of about 3.333333 and 0.198020 percentage points. These are sensitivity calculations, not confidence intervals.
4.practice: Change one success to a failure in samples 4/5 and 80/100; calculate both new rates and identify the sampling assumptions needed for population inference.

questions.question: What are the revised rates?
Is the one-observation sensitivity a confidence interval?
questions.answer: No. A confidence interval requires a specified method and sampling assumptions.

4.mistake: Changing an existing outcome keeps n fixed; appending a new trial increases n. Confusing them gives the wrong rate change. Equal sample fractions also do not imply equal uncertainty, and a larger biased sample can still mislead.

4.title: Optimization and numerical checks
4.objective: Compute binary log loss under finite-probability and boundary inputs.
4.idea: An objective gives the quantity an optimizer tries to reduce or increase. Binary log loss penalizes assigning low probability to the observed outcome, while stable numerical methods avoid unnecessary overflow or underflow. Constraints, nonconvexity and finite precision mean that an optimizer result needs checks rather than an automatic global-optimum claim.
4.example: For target y=1, loss=−ln(p). At p=0.5 the loss is about 0.693; at p=0.9 it is about 0.105; ln(0) is not finite and the loss grows without bound as p approaches zero.
4.practice: Compute −ln(p) for p=0.25 and p=0.75 with a calculator or Python; state an explicit policy for a supplied probability of zero.

questions.question: Which probability has lower loss for y=1?
questions.answer: 0.75, because it assigns more probability to the observed outcome.

questions.question: Does clipping leave the loss formula unchanged?
questions.answer: No. Clipping changes the calculation and must be documented.

4.mistake: A stationary point in a nonconvex objective is not automatically a global optimum.

5.title: Formats, acquisition and queries
5.objective: Compare CSV and JSON representations of the same two records.
5.idea: Structured tables use consistent columns, while JSON can represent nested values. A file format does not guarantee valid types, correct measurements or permission to use the records. SQL filters and joins relational data, while warehouses and lakes organize analytical storage in different ways.
5.example: CSV age values arrive as text such as "20" or an empty string. JSON can express {"age":20} or {"age":null}; neither representation supplies a missing age automatically.
5.practice: Represent two synthetic customers, one with unknown age, in CSV and JSON; state the parsing and validation policy for both.

questions.question: Is an empty CSV field numeric zero?
questions.answer: No. Missing and zero are different values.

questions.question: Does having a dataset grant unrestricted usage rights?
questions.answer: No. Collection, permission and licensing constraints still apply.

5.mistake: Parsing a file successfully does not establish data quality or provenance.

5.title: Cleaning and transformations
5.objective: Diagnose missing, duplicate and conflicting records before transformation.
5.idea: An exact duplicate repeats every field, while conflicting rows may share an identifier with different values. Cleaning needs an explicit policy that preserves raw data and exposes rejected records. Scaling and encoding alter model inputs; they must be fitted using the appropriate training data.
5.example: Rows (id=1,age=20), (id=1,age=20) and (id=1,age=21) contain one exact duplicate plus a conflicting age for the same ID. Dropping every repeated ID would hide the conflict.
5.practice: Profile three synthetic rows with an exact duplicate and a conflicting identifier; produce separate duplicate, missing and conflict counts before cleaning.

questions.question: Should the first repeated ID always win?
questions.answer: No. Conflicts require an explicit resolution or quarantine policy.

questions.question: Should a scaler learn validation-data statistics?
questions.answer: No. Fit learned preprocessing on training data and apply it to held-out data.

5.mistake: An unusual value is not automatically an error; investigate the measurement and task before deleting outliers.

5.title: Exploration, labels and evaluation
5.objective: Diagnose an evaluation split contaminated by repeated examples.
5.idea: Exploration reveals distributions and candidate quality problems but can influence later decisions. Labels define the target, and train, validation and test partitions serve different purposes. Reusing a test result to tune the system consumes its independence; duplicates across splits can also exaggerate generalization.
5.example: A customer record copied into train and test lets a memorizing system appear correct on the repeated record. Grouping duplicates before assigning partitions prevents that exact overlap.
5.practice: Create six records with one duplicate pair, assign a group-aware split, and list which examples may influence fitting, selection and final evaluation.

questions.question: May test labels guide feature selection?
questions.answer: No. That leaks evaluation information into development.

questions.question: Does a plot prove a causal relationship?
questions.answer: No. It shows an observed association under the dataset conditions.

5.mistake: A balanced-looking split can still leak when related records from the same entity cross partitions.

5.title: Lineage, privacy and pipelines
5.objective: Implement a small data-quality contract with traceable inputs.
5.idea: Lineage records where a dataset came from and which transformations produced it. Versioning makes a particular input recoverable, while a pipeline applies repeatable processing stages. Privacy requires considering identifiers, access and retention; removing names alone may not prevent identification.
5.example: A manifest records raw.csv version A, the cleaning policy and clean.csv version B. If B has fewer rows, a rejection report should explain the difference.
5.practice: Write a manifest for a synthetic CSV pipeline with input version, row counts, rejection reasons, access policy and retention rule.

questions.question: Does removing names guarantee anonymity?
questions.answer: No. Other fields and combinations may still identify people.

questions.question: Why retain rejected-row counts?
questions.answer: They make transformations auditable and can reveal silent data loss.

5.mistake: A filename such as latest.csv is not a reproducible dataset version by itself.

6.title: Agents, states and search problems
6.objective: Implement a finite state-space description for a route problem.
6.idea: A search problem needs states, actions, transition rules and a goal test. An agent selects actions under its observations and performance criterion. A useful state contains what future decisions need, without assuming that the agent knows every hidden fact.
6.example: States A,B,C have edges A→B and B→C; start A and goal C. The action sequence A→B→C reaches the goal in two moves.
6.practice: Specify a four-location route graph, allowed actions and one unreachable goal; distinguish state from the path taken to reach it.

questions.question: Is a goal description an algorithm?
questions.answer: No. It states success but not how to find it.

questions.question: Can incomplete observations affect rational action?
questions.answer: Yes. Decisions depend on available information and the criterion.

6.mistake: A search state is a modeling choice, not necessarily a full copy of the real world.

6.title: Uninformed and heuristic search
6.objective: Compare breadth-first and cost-based search on a small graph.
6.idea: Breadth-first search prioritizes depth and finds a shortest edge-count path under appropriate finite-branching conditions. Uniform-cost search prioritizes cumulative cost, while A* combines path cost with a heuristic. A heuristic guarantee depends on its assumptions and the search implementation, not merely its plausibility.
6.example: A→G costs 10; A→B costs 1 and B→G costs 1. Breadth-first can find the one-edge route, while uniform-cost prefers the two-edge cost-2 route.
6.practice: Trace queue removals for both searches on this graph, then use h=0 to explain the connection between A* and uniform-cost search.

questions.question: Does fewest edges always mean lowest cost?
questions.answer: No. Edge weights may differ.

questions.question: What does h=0 contribute?
questions.answer: No estimated remaining cost; A* then orders by accumulated cost.

6.mistake: An overestimating heuristic can invalidate the usual optimality guarantee.

6.title: Local, adversarial and constraint search
6.objective: Compare a local-search optimum with a constraint-satisfaction result.
6.idea: Local search improves a candidate using nearby alternatives but may become trapped. Adversarial search considers another player choices, while constraint satisfaction requires assignments meeting stated restrictions. These are different problem formulations, even when all explore alternatives.
6.example: Assign colors to adjacent nodes A–B. A=red,B=red violates the different-color constraint; changing B to blue satisfies it.
6.practice: List valid two-colorings for A–B–C and one invalid assignment; explain how a third edge C–A changes feasibility.

questions.question: Can a two-color triangle satisfy all unequal-neighbor constraints?
questions.answer: No. The odd cycle requires more than two colors.

questions.question: Is a local optimum necessarily global?
questions.answer: No. Better solutions may exist beyond local moves.

6.mistake: Pruning is correct only when the discarded alternatives cannot affect the required result.

6.title: Symbols, rules and knowledge
6.objective: Trace a rule-based conclusion from explicit facts.
6.idea: Knowledge representations encode entities, relations and rules. Logical inference derives consequences under the stated formal semantics, while ontologies and graphs organize concepts and connections. A formally derived conclusion is only as applicable as its premises and model of the world.
6.example: Facts: bird(tweety), and rule bird(x)→animal(x). The rule derives animal(tweety); it does not derive can_fly(tweety) without another premise.
6.practice: Create three facts and two rules for synthetic library items; trace exactly which conclusions follow and which do not.

questions.question: Can missing evidence be treated as false in every logic?
questions.answer: No. That depends on the chosen semantics and assumptions.

questions.question: Does a rule establish real-world truth if its premise is wrong?
questions.answer: No. Formal validity does not verify the premises.

6.mistake: Confusing a plausible rule with an exception-free fact can produce invalid application decisions.

6.title: Planning and uncertain decisions
6.objective: Compute expected value for two actions under stated probabilities.
6.idea: Planning models actions and their effects, while uncertain decisions also need probability and utility assumptions. Bayesian networks and hidden-state models represent dependencies and observations. MDP and POMDP formulations differ in whether the decision state is fully observed.
6.example: Action A pays 10 with probability 0.5 and 0 otherwise, giving expected payoff 5. Action B pays 4 certainly; expected-payoff maximization chooses A under these stated values.
6.practice: Change A success probability to 0.3 and recompute; explain why a risk constraint could change the decision even at equal expected value.

questions.question: What is A revised expected payoff?
Is expected payoff a guaranteed realized payoff?
questions.answer: No. Individual outcomes can differ.

6.mistake: A decision-theory result depends on the modeled utilities and probabilities, not only the arithmetic.

7.title: Learning tasks and representations
7.objective: Compare classification, regression and unsupervised tasks for a tiny dataset.
7.idea: Supervised learning uses labeled examples, while unsupervised learning finds structure without that target supervision. Self-supervision derives a training signal from the data, and reinforcement learning concerns actions and reward. Training changes a model; inference applies it to new inputs under a defined feature contract.
7.example: Predicting a numeric house price is regression; predicting spam/not spam is classification. Grouping unlabeled messages by similarity is clustering, and those groups are not automatically spam classes.
7.practice: Define features and targets for a numeric forecast and a binary classification task; explain how online versus batch updates change the training workflow.

questions.question: Are clusters guaranteed to match target classes?
questions.answer: No. Similarity groups need not align with the intended labels.

questions.question: Is inference the same as training?
questions.answer: No. Ordinary inference uses the fitted model rather than fitting it.

7.mistake: A parameter count or model family does not by itself determine whether the task is classification or regression.

7.title: Loss, fit and generalization
7.objective: Compute training error and held-out error for two candidate predictions.
7.idea: A loss scores prediction error, and empirical risk averages it over observed training examples. Low training loss can coexist with high held-out loss when a model overfits. Regularization restricts fitting behavior but requires evaluation; the bias-variance tradeoff describes sources of predictive error rather than a guaranteed tuning recipe.
7.example: For targets [1,3], predictions [1,3] give mean squared error 0; predictions [2,2] give mean squared error 1. Perfect fit on these two examples alone says nothing about a new input.
7.practice: Construct two training predictions and two validation predictions for a memorizing and a simple model; compute both mean squared errors and choose using validation evidence.

questions.question: Does zero training error establish generalization?
questions.answer: No. Evaluate data not used for fitting.

questions.question: Is regularization guaranteed to improve every dataset?
questions.answer: No. Its effect must be evaluated for the task and configuration.

7.mistake: Selecting a model using test error turns the test set into development information.

7.title: Selection, validation and baselines
7.objective: Compare candidate models with a baseline using separated selection data.
7.idea: A baseline provides a simple comparison, such as majority-class prediction. Cross-validation repeats training and evaluation on planned folds, and all learned preprocessing belongs inside each training fold. Hyperparameters are selected using development evidence; a final test partition is reserved for evaluation after selection.
7.example: Labels [0,0,0,1] give a majority-class accuracy of 3/4=75% when always predicting 0. A candidate scoring 75% on the same cases has not improved that metric over this baseline.
7.practice: Create a four-fold evaluation plan with a majority-class baseline, fold-level scores and a final untouched test set; identify where preprocessing is fitted.

questions.question: Does a 75% score beat a 75% baseline?
questions.answer: No. It matches that measured metric on those cases.

questions.question: Can preprocessing be fitted before creating folds?
questions.answer: No. Learned statistics would include held-out fold information.

7.mistake: A cross-validation standard deviation describes fold-score variation; it is not automatically a confidence interval.

7.title: Imbalance, interpretation and workflow
7.objective: Diagnose a high-accuracy classifier that misses every rare positive.
7.idea: Class imbalance can make accuracy hide important failures. Augmentation changes the training examples and must preserve the relevant meaning and partition boundaries. Interpretation helps inspect behavior, but an explanation method does not establish causal effects or fairness.
7.example: With 99 negatives and 1 positive, always-negative predictions yield 99% accuracy and zero recall for positives. The desired metric depends on the consequences of that missed positive.
7.practice: Build a confusion table for an always-negative classifier on 20 cases with two positives; propose a metric and an error-review workflow.

questions.question: Can high accuracy coexist with zero positive recall?
questions.answer: Yes. It happens when the majority class dominates and every positive is missed.

questions.question: Does a feature attribution prove causation?
questions.answer: No. It describes a model behavior under the method assumptions.

7.mistake: Apply resampling only within training partitions; copying minority rows into held-out data leaks examples.

8.title: Regression and regularized objectives
8.objective: Compare prediction error and a regularization penalty for two linear fits.
8.idea: Linear regression models a numeric target, while polynomial features let a linear-in-parameters model represent curved relationships. Ridge and lasso add different coefficient penalties; elastic net combines them. Flexible models such as Gaussian processes express additional assumptions and uncertainty that need checking against the task.
8.example: Reference expectation: use x=[1,2], y=[1,3], prediction w×x, no intercept, and objective J=MSE+λw² with λ=0.5. Candidate A has w=1, predictions [1,2], MSE=(0²+1²)/2=0.5 and penalty 0.5×1²=0.5, so J=1.0. Candidate B has w=1.5, predictions [1.5,3], MSE=(0.5²+0²)/2=0.125 and penalty 0.5×1.5²=1.125, so J=1.25. Among these two candidates, A has the lower penalized objective even though B fits these targets better; this is not a claim that A is the global minimizer.
8.practice: Recompute both candidates for λ=0.1 using the same x and y; report each MSE, coefficient penalty and total objective, then identify the lower-objective candidate.

questions.question: Which candidate has the lower objective at λ=0.5, and why?
questions.answer: A: J=1.0 versus B: J=1.25. Its smaller coefficient penalty outweighs its larger MSE under this specified objective.

questions.question: What happens to these two objectives when λ becomes 0.1?
questions.answer: A has J=0.5+0.1=0.6; B has J=0.125+0.225=0.35. B is now preferred among these candidates; changing λ changes the fit-versus-penalty tradeoff.

8.mistake: MSE and a penalized training objective are different quantities. A lower MSE alone does not guarantee a lower penalized objective, and comparing two candidates does not prove a global optimum.

8.title: Classification decision mechanisms
8.objective: Compare neighbor, linear-boundary and tree decisions on a tiny classification task.
8.idea: Logistic regression models a class probability through a link function, while nearest neighbors uses nearby training examples. Trees partition feature space with decisions, and Naive Bayes uses a conditional-independence modeling assumption. Support vector methods use margins and can apply kernels; the choice still needs a baseline and cross-validated evidence.
8.example: A one-nearest-neighbor classifier sees labeled points 0:A and 10:B. Query 2 is nearer 0 and receives A under absolute distance; this rule depends on feature scaling.
8.practice: Trace 1-NN predictions for queries 2 and 8, then describe one tree threshold that matches these two decisions and a boundary case.

questions.question: Does Naive Bayes require all features to be unconditionally independent?
questions.answer: No. Its standard simplifying assumption is conditional independence given the class.

questions.question: Does a distance model ignore feature units?
questions.answer: No. Units and scaling can dominate distances.

8.mistake: Logistic regression is used for classification despite the word regression in its name.

8.title: Ensembles and controlled comparison
8.objective: Compute a cross-validation comparison against a baseline from per-fold scores.
8.idea: Bagging aggregates learners fitted to resampled training data, while boosting and stacking combine learners under different training rules. Ensemble members can share errors, so more models do not guarantee better held-out quality. Compare a baseline and candidate models on the same folds with every learned preprocessing step fitted inside that fold training data. The worked report below uses given synthetic fold errors to teach aggregation; it is not a claim that those models were trained or measured here. Sample standard deviation describes variation across these folds and is not a confidence interval for future performance.
8.example:
Reference expectation — synthetic fold-score arithmetic, not an executed training run. Assume three fixed folds and MAE in the same target units; labels identify hypothetical candidates only.
Candidate                 Fold 1  Fold 2  Fold 3  Mean MAE  Sample SD
Training-mean baseline       4       5       6       5        1
Linear-model candidate      2       3       4       3        1
Tree-model candidate        1       3       2       2        1
Bagged-tree candidate       2       2       5       3        1.732051
For the bagged candidate, sample SD=sqrt(((2−3)²+(2−3)²+(5−3)²)/(3−1))=sqrt(3)≈1.732051. The tree candidate has the lowest mean MAE in this given fixture; these data do not establish a general model ranking. Separately, binary votes [1,1,0] yield class 1 by majority vote, illustrating aggregation rather than a regression score.
8.practice: Produce the same baseline-versus-three-model report after changing the bagged candidate third-fold MAE from 5 to 8. For an optional scikit-learn implementation, fit three models and a simple baseline on identical k-fold splits with fold-local preprocessing; replace the given scores with actual recorded fold scores and report mean ± sample standard deviation.

questions.question: What are the tree candidate mean MAE and sample SD in the original table?
questions.answer: Mean=(1+3+2)/3=2; sample SD=sqrt(((1−2)²+(3−2)²+(2−2)²)/(3−1))=1, so the report is 2 ± 1 target units.

questions.question: Why is the bagged candidate report 3 ± 1.732051 not a confidence interval?
questions.answer: It reports the mean and sample SD of three supplied fold errors. Folds can be dependent through overlapping training data; this spread is not a calibrated interval for future model quality.

8.mistake: Do not present supplied synthetic fold errors as observed training results. A favorable three-fold mean and its sample SD do not prove superiority on a new population or replace an independent evaluation.

8.title: Tabular neural models and validation
8.objective: Diagnose a tabular neural model comparison without a simple baseline.
8.idea: A neural model can learn feature interactions but adds training and tuning choices. Tabular datasets often require careful missing-value and categorical handling before fitting. Use the same leakage-safe folds, target metric and resource accounting for a neural model and simpler baselines.
8.example: A neural classifier reaches 9/10 correct while an always-majority baseline also reaches 9/10. The reported accuracy does not demonstrate an improvement.
8.practice: Write a fair comparison plan for a tabular neural model, a simple tree and a baseline including identical folds, preprocessing, score variation and training budget.

questions.question: Does 90% accuracy necessarily beat a baseline?
questions.answer: No. Measure the baseline on the same evaluation cases.

questions.question: May neural-model preprocessing see held-out rows?
questions.answer: No. Learned preprocessing must stay within training folds.

8.mistake: A larger neural network is not automatically the best choice for a small tabular dataset.

9.title: Clusters and density structure
9.objective: Compare a centroid assignment with a density-based noise decision.
9.idea: Clustering groups observations under a selected representation and criterion rather than recovering guaranteed natural labels. K-Means minimizes squared distances to centroids and needs a chosen cluster count. Density, hierarchy and mixture methods make other assumptions, and noise points need not be forced into a meaningful group.
9.example: Points [0,1,9,10] with centroids 0.5 and 9.5 form two clear nearest-centroid groups. An isolated point 100 can strongly move a mean, illustrating sensitivity to outliers.
9.practice: Assign [0,1,9,10,100] to stated initial centroids, recompute means and explain how a density approach could treat the isolated point differently.

questions.question: Does a cluster number imply a semantic class?
questions.answer: No. Interpret and validate it using domain evidence.

questions.question: Is K-Means insensitive to an extreme point?
questions.answer: No. Squared-distance fitting can be strongly affected.

9.mistake: Changing feature scale can change the discovered groups without changing the underlying records.

9.title: Reduced representations
9.objective: Compare variance preservation with neighborhood visualization.
9.idea: Dimensionality reduction creates a lower-dimensional representation with a method-specific objective. PCA preserves directions of high variance in a linear projection, while nonlinear visualization methods emphasize other structures. A two-dimensional picture can distort distances and is not independent evidence of true clusters.
9.example: For points on the line y=x, a projection along that diagonal preserves their one-dimensional variation. Projecting onto a perpendicular direction loses that variation.
9.practice: Project three points on y=x onto the diagonal and a perpendicular direction; explain which distinctions remain and why visualization should not be treated as a classifier.

questions.question: Does high variance always mean task relevance?
questions.answer: No. Variance can reflect nuisance variation.

questions.question: Can distances in a visualization be read as exact original distances?
questions.answer: No. Check the method objective and distortions.

9.mistake: Fitting a representation on a final evaluation set can leak information into a downstream supervised comparison.

9.title: Associations and anomalies
9.objective: Diagnose an association rule interpreted as a causal or security claim.
9.idea: Association rules summarize co-occurrence under a chosen counting scheme. Anomaly detection identifies unusual observations under a fitted notion of normality, not automatically fraud or error. Thresholds and alert workloads need evaluation with available labels and human review.
9.example: If 4 of 10 baskets contain tea and 3 of those also contain milk, confidence of tea→milk is 3/4=75% and support of the pair is 3/10=30%. This is not a causal effect.
9.practice: Compute support and confidence for a small synthetic basket table, then propose how an unusual-basket alert would be reviewed rather than automatically called fraud.

questions.question: Does 75% rule confidence mean tea causes milk purchases?
questions.answer: No. It is a conditional co-occurrence rate.

questions.question: Is every anomaly malicious?
questions.answer: No. Rare legitimate events can also be unusual.

9.mistake: A low anomaly score is not a calibrated probability of fraud unless that interpretation has been established.

10.title: Splits and cross-validation
10.objective: Diagnose a split that allows future information into training.
10.idea: A train partition fits parameters, validation guides choices, and a test partition evaluates the selected process. K-fold and stratified folds depend on suitable independence assumptions; time-dependent data needs an order-respecting design. Search methods differ in how they propose candidates, not in whether evaluation leakage is acceptable.
10.example: A forecast for March cannot train on an April outcome. Rolling-origin evaluation trains on the past, predicts a later interval, then advances the origin.
10.practice: Specify a split plan for independent customer records and a second plan for monthly forecasting; name the baseline and one leakage check in each.

questions.question: Can stratification repair temporal leakage?
questions.answer: No. Preserving class proportions does not enforce time order.

questions.question: May the test set choose the search winner?
questions.answer: No. Reserve it for evaluating the already selected process.

10.mistake: A reproducible random seed does not make an invalid split valid.

10.title: Confusion matrix and threshold tradeoffs
10.objective: Compute precision, recall and F1 from a confusion matrix.
10.idea: A confusion matrix separates true positives, false positives, true negatives and false negatives. Precision concerns predicted positives, while recall concerns actual positives. Threshold curves compare operating points, and the useful tradeoff depends on error costs and prevalence.
10.practice: Change FP to 4 while holding the other counts fixed; recompute precision, recall, F1 and total count, then explain which denominator changed.

questions.question: Does precision use every actual positive in its denominator?
questions.answer: No. It uses predicted positives, TP+FP.

questions.question: Can two thresholds have different recall on one score set?
questions.answer: Yes. A lower positive threshold typically includes more examples.

10.mistake: AUC summarizes ranking across thresholds; it does not specify the operational threshold or its error costs.

10.title: Calibration and metric meaning
10.objective: Compare predicted confidence with observed frequency in a small bin.
10.idea: Calibration asks whether events assigned a probability occur at a similar observed frequency. Regression errors, clustering scores and ranking metrics answer different task questions and need stated units or relevance labels. Proper probability scoring rules such as log loss penalize confident mistakes, but a small calibration bin is noisy.
10.example: Ten predictions each assign probability 0.8; six outcomes are positive. This bin has mean forecast 0.8, observed frequency 0.6 and an observed gap of 0.2, without enough evidence for a stable population conclusion.
10.practice: Create two probability bins with ten synthetic cases each; calculate mean forecast and outcome frequency, then describe the sample-size limitation.

questions.question: Does 0.8 probability guarantee one event occurs?
questions.answer: No. Calibration concerns frequencies over comparable cases.

questions.question: Does lower RMSE have units?
questions.answer: Yes. RMSE has the target variable units.

10.mistake: Good discrimination does not imply calibrated probabilities, and binning choices can hide calibration defects.

10.title: Ablation, uncertainty and error analysis
10.objective: Diagnose an apparent improvement without a baseline or uncertainty estimate.
10.idea: An ablation changes a component while holding the comparison conditions as stable as possible. Error analysis examines failure categories rather than just a single aggregate score. Report a baseline, sample size and an uncertainty estimate suitable for the data and dependence structure; statistical significance is not practical importance.
10.example: A system improves from 8/10 to 9/10 correct on a reused development set. The one-case difference is descriptive evidence, not a demonstrated reliable gain on new users.
10.practice: Write a baseline-versus-candidate report including identical cases, paired errors, sample size, an appropriate confidence-interval plan and one important failure slice.

questions.question: Is one extra correct case proof of a reliable improvement?
questions.answer: No. Sampling uncertainty and the evaluation design matter.

questions.question: Does a p-value measure the probability the null hypothesis is true?
questions.answer: No. It concerns data at least as incompatible with the null under its assumptions.

10.mistake: Reporting only the best run hides selection effects and uncertainty.

11.title: Transformations and leakage-safe preprocessing
11.objective: Diagnose a preprocessing statistic fitted outside the training partition.
11.idea: Scaling, encoding and imputation learn or apply rules to feature values. Fit learned statistics on training data and reuse them for held-out inputs. Pipelines preserve this sequence during cross-validation, while feature interactions and selection must also respect the fitting boundary.
11.example: Training ages [20,40] have mean 30; an unseen age 100 must not change that fitted mean to a rounded 53.33 before evaluation. The imputation or centering rule belongs to the training partition.
11.practice: Write a fit/transform trace for training values [2,4] and validation value 10; calculate the training mean and show the held-out transform without refitting.

questions.question: What is the training mean?
May feature selection use validation labels inside every fold?
questions.answer: No. Selection must be fitted within the fold training data.

11.mistake: A pipeline prevents leakage only if its components and evaluation boundaries are configured correctly.

11.title: Imbalance, resampling and augmentation
11.objective: Diagnose duplicated minority examples crossing a validation boundary.
11.idea: Resampling changes the training distribution to address a learning objective. Synthetic oversampling and augmentation can leak if derived examples cross evaluation boundaries. Evaluate the actual target distribution and report threshold-specific behavior rather than treating resampled class proportions as deployment prevalence.
11.example: A minority row is copied into both train and validation. A memorizing classifier can now score well on the copy without learning to generalize.
11.practice: Plan fold-local resampling for a 9:1 synthetic class ratio; identify which originals and generated examples must remain outside each validation fold.

questions.question: Should validation data be oversampled to hide imbalance?
questions.answer: No. Preserve a justified evaluation distribution and report relevant metrics.

questions.question: Can augmentation change the label meaning?
questions.answer: Yes. Validate that the transformation preserves the intended target.

11.mistake: Resampling before splitting can create exact or near-duplicate leakage.

11.title: Applied-task contracts
11.objective: Compare evaluation boundaries for forecasting, ranking and fraud detection.
11.idea: A feature is usable only if it exists at prediction time. Forecasting requires temporal availability, while recommendation and ranking require candidate and relevance definitions. Fraud and maintenance tasks often have delayed outcomes, so training labels and evaluation windows need explicit timing.
11.example: Using final account closure status to predict an earlier fraud event introduces future information. The field may be present in an exported table but unavailable at the actual decision time.
11.practice: Choose a synthetic maintenance alert task and create a feature-availability table with event time, availability time, label delay and split policy.

questions.question: Does a column in an export necessarily exist at prediction time?
questions.answer: No. Check when it became available.

questions.question: Can random row splits always evaluate forecasting?
questions.answer: No. They can mix past and future or related observations.

11.mistake: High offline scores can reflect future-derived features rather than a useful prediction system.

11.title: Interpretation, fairness and causal claims
11.objective: Diagnose a feature attribution presented as a causal explanation.
11.idea: Interpretability methods describe aspects of model behavior under their assumptions. SHAP and LIME outputs do not by themselves identify what would happen under a real intervention. Fairness analysis and A/B tests require task-specific populations, assignment rules and uncertainty reporting.
11.example: A model associates umbrella ownership with rain. Removing umbrellas does not prevent rain; predictive association is not a causal mechanism.
11.practice: Write a model explanation and a separate causal hypothesis for a synthetic churn prediction; state the experiment or assumptions needed to test the causal claim.

questions.question: Does a positive feature attribution prove an intervention effect?
questions.answer: No. It explains model behavior, not necessarily causation.

questions.question: Does one aggregate fairness score cover every group?
questions.answer: No. Inspect relevant groups and metric definitions.

11.mistake: An explanation that sounds intuitive can still be unstable or irrelevant to a decision.

12.title: Neurons, activations and forward passes
12.objective: Compute a single-neuron forward pass with a ReLU activation.
12.idea: A neuron applies weights and a bias before a nonlinear activation. Stacking layers composes transformations; without suitable nonlinearities, multiple linear layers collapse to a linear transformation. Activations such as sigmoid, tanh, ReLU and softmax serve different roles and have different numerical properties.
12.example: For x=[2,−1], w=[1,3] and bias 2, preactivation is 2−3+2=1. ReLU returns max(0,1)=1.
12.practice: Compute the same neuron for x=[−2,1] and x=[0,0], then compare the result with and without ReLU.

questions.question: What is the preactivation for [−2,1]?
questions.answer: −2+3+2=3, so ReLU returns 3.

questions.question: Does ReLU return a probability distribution?
questions.answer: No. Its output is nonnegative but not normalized as probabilities.

12.mistake: Artificial neurons are mathematical components, not faithful models of every biological-neuron mechanism.

12.title: Losses, gradients and training
12.objective: Compute a gradient step using a stated learning rate.
12.idea: A loss compares predictions with targets, and backpropagation applies the chain rule through a computation graph. Automatic differentiation calculates these derivatives but does not choose the right objective. Gradient-based optimizers update parameters from gradients; mini-batches and adaptive methods change the update behavior and noise.
12.example: For prediction w*x, x=1, y=3 and loss (w−3)^2 at w=0, gradient is −6. A step with rate 0.1 gives w=0.6 and loss 5.76; rate 2 gives w=12 and loss 81.
12.practice: Trace three updates for the quadratic with rate 0.1; record parameter, gradient and loss each time, then contrast the first update at rate 2.

questions.question: Does subtracting a negative gradient increase w here?
Does automatic differentiation guarantee a useful model?
questions.answer: No. Data, objective, architecture and evaluation still matter.

12.mistake: A high learning rate can make loss diverge; do not hide it by reporting only the initial step.

12.title: Stability, normalization and regularization
12.objective: Diagnose a training run with falling training loss and rising validation loss.
12.idea: Initialization and normalization affect signal and gradient behavior across layers. Dropout, weight decay and early stopping constrain training in different ways. Regularization should be assessed using development data; a held-out test set should not select the stopping point.
12.example: Training losses [3,2,1] and validation losses [3,2.2,2.8] suggest that the third checkpoint worsens validation performance despite better training fit. Under these observations, checkpoint two has the lowest listed validation loss.
12.practice: Create a checkpoint-selection rule for the listed losses and record what further evaluation is needed; distinguish normalization from weight decay.

questions.question: Which listed checkpoint has the lowest validation loss?
questions.answer: The second, with 2.2.

questions.question: May test loss choose an early-stopping epoch?
questions.answer: No. That uses test information for selection.

12.mistake: Dropout and weight decay are not interchangeable operations merely because both can regularize.

12.title: Architecture connections and compute
12.objective: Compare a residual addition with an ordinary layer transformation.
12.idea: Residual and skip connections provide alternative information paths through a network. Embedding layers learn vector representations, while GPU and mixed-precision execution change how operations are computed. Lower precision can improve resource use but needs stability and output-quality checks under the actual hardware and framework.
12.example: A residual block returning x+f(x) with x=2 and f(x)=0.5 outputs 2.5. If f(x)=0 it preserves x, unlike replacing x with f(x).
12.practice: Trace an identity residual block and a nonzero block; write checks for shape agreement and a precision change in a hypothetical training run.

questions.question: Can arbitrary tensor shapes always be added?
questions.answer: No. They must satisfy the framework addition and broadcasting rules.

questions.question: Does GPU execution guarantee identical floating-point results?
questions.answer: No. Algorithms and precision can differ.

12.mistake: A lower-precision run requires measured quality and stability evidence, not only a speed claim.

12.title: Checkpoints and debugging
12.objective: Diagnose a resumed run with missing optimizer state.
12.idea: A checkpoint may contain weights, optimizer state, training position and configuration. Saving weights alone can support inference but may not reproduce a training continuation. Debugging should check a tiny batch, labels, shapes and loss behavior before increasing model size or compute.
12.example: A resumed adaptive-optimizer run loads weights but resets its moment estimates. It can continue, yet it is not the same optimizer state as an uninterrupted run.
12.practice: Write a checkpoint manifest and a tiny-batch debugging checklist; state which saved fields are required for inference versus training continuation.

questions.question: Are weights alone enough to reproduce every training continuation?
questions.answer: No. Optimizer, scheduler and other state may matter.

questions.question: Why test a tiny batch first?
questions.answer: It exposes shape, label and update failures with a tractable trace.

12.mistake: A saved file is not a verified checkpoint until loading and intended use have been tested.

13.title: Dense and convolutional feature extraction
13.objective: Compute a one-dimensional convolution-style feature trace.
13.idea: Dense layers connect all selected input features to outputs. Convolutional layers reuse local weights across positions, while pooling aggregates nearby responses. Named architecture families organize these operations differently, so compare an actual configuration rather than assuming its name establishes task quality.
13.example: Using cross-correlation weights [1,−1] on [3,1,4] with stride 1 and no padding gives [2,−3]. This simple trace illustrates weight sharing, not a complete image model.
13.practice: Trace weights [1,1] on [2,0,3,1], then max-pool adjacent output pairs under a stated policy for an unmatched last value.

questions.question: Why is the same filter reused?
questions.answer: To apply one learned local pattern detector across positions.

questions.question: Does pooling preserve every exact location?
questions.answer: No. Aggregation can discard spatial detail.

13.mistake: Framework convolution layers commonly implement cross-correlation; state the convention before a hand calculation.

13.title: Recurrent and sequence-to-sequence models
13.objective: Trace information flow through a recurrent sequence model.
13.idea: A recurrent model updates hidden state as it reads a sequence. LSTM and GRU designs control information flow with gates but still require suitable training and evaluation. Encoder-decoder models map an input representation to an output sequence, possibly of a different length.
13.example: For the illustrative recurrence h_t=h_(t−1)+x_t with h_0=0 and inputs [2,−1,3], states are [2,1,4]. A real learned recurrence adds parameters and nonlinearities.
13.practice: Trace the recurrence for [1,2,−2] and explain what final-state compression can lose about input order.

questions.question: Can different sequences share the same summed final state?
questions.answer: Yes. [1,2] and [2,1] both sum to 3.

questions.question: Do gates guarantee unlimited memory?
questions.answer: No. Evaluate retention on the actual task and sequence lengths.

13.mistake: A simple state-sum teaching trace is not an LSTM implementation.

13.title: Attention and Transformer families
13.objective: Compare permitted context in encoder and causal-decoder attention.
13.idea: Attention weights combine value representations based on queries and keys. Encoder-style and causal-decoder-style models use different context visibility. An encoder-decoder design also lets decoder states attend to encoded input, but each specific model may vary.
13.example: At position 2, a causal mask allows positions 1 and 2 but blocks position 3. A bidirectional encoder can use later input positions under its stated mask.
13.practice: Draw a three-token allowed-attention table for causal and bidirectional masks; explain which could leak a future target in next-token training.

questions.question: May causal attention inspect a later target token?
questions.answer: No. That would violate the intended prediction boundary.

questions.question: Is cross-attention identical to self-attention?
questions.answer: No. Queries and key/value context come from different representations.

13.mistake: The word Transformer does not specify one universal masking or input-output contract.

13.title: Latent, graph and alternative architectures
13.objective: Compare representation assumptions in an autoencoder and a graph network.
13.idea: Autoencoders reconstruct inputs through learned representations, while variational autoencoders add a probabilistic latent formulation. Graph networks pass information along graph relations, and Siamese designs compare representations through shared or related encoders. Mixture-of-experts, state-space and differential-equation architectures change computation in other ways and require task-specific evidence.
13.example: A graph with edges A–B and B–C gives A direct access to B in one local message-passing step. C may influence A after additional steps, depending on the update rule.
13.practice: Trace two rounds of neighbor-sum messages on A–B–C with initial values [1,2,3]; state whether self-values are included.

questions.question: Does a reconstruction objective guarantee useful class labels?
questions.answer: No. Reconstruction and classification optimize different criteria.

questions.question: Can graph edges leak evaluation information?
questions.answer: Yes. Build and split the graph according to the evaluation boundary.

13.mistake: Architecture novelty alone does not establish a better baseline comparison.

14.title: Text normalization and linguistic structure
14.objective: Diagnose a normalization rule that changes meaning.
14.idea: Text preprocessing selects which distinctions the representation keeps. Tokenization, stemming and lemmatization serve different purposes, while syntax and semantic interpretation add task-specific structure. Removing words or punctuation can destroy negation, identifiers or boundaries needed for the task.
14.example: Removing "not" from "not approved" changes the apparent meaning to "approved". A stop-word list must therefore be evaluated against the actual decision task.
14.practice: Create three short sentences where lowercasing, punctuation removal or stop-word deletion changes a useful distinction; propose a safer policy.

questions.question: Are stemming and lemmatization identical?
questions.answer: No. Stemming applies form-reduction rules; lemmatization seeks a lexical base form using linguistic information.

questions.question: Should every task remove stop words?
questions.answer: No. Important signals such as negation may be removed.

14.mistake: A cleaned-looking string can be less faithful to the source than the original.

14.title: Sparse and learned representations
14.objective: Compare bag-of-words counts with a contextual representation.
14.idea: Bag-of-words counts terms while discarding much order information. TF-IDF adjusts term weights using document statistics, and learned embeddings represent distributional patterns. Static word vectors and contextual representations differ because context can change the representation of the same token.
14.example: "dog bites person" and "person bites dog" have the same bag-of-words counts. Their meanings differ because word order and roles differ.
14.practice: Build term counts for the two sentences and a third sentence; identify a decision that term counts alone cannot make reliably.

questions.question: Does equal bag-of-words mean equal sentence meaning?
questions.answer: No. Order and relationships may differ.

questions.question: May IDF statistics use a reserved test collection during model selection?
questions.answer: Not in a strictly held-out inductive evaluation; fit the representation under the stated boundary.

14.mistake: Embedding closeness reflects a learned representation, not a dictionary guarantee of synonymy.

14.title: Prediction tasks and sequence labels
14.objective: Compare a document label with token-level entity annotations.
14.idea: Text classification assigns labels to a text unit, while sequence labeling assigns labels to positions or spans. Topic models discover patterns under their assumptions rather than guaranteed business categories. Language modeling predicts text structure and is not the same as a sentiment classifier.
14.example: "Ada works in Oslo" can have a document label work-related and entity spans Ada=person, Oslo=location. These are different targets and need different evaluation units.
14.practice: Annotate three synthetic sentences with one document label and entity spans; write rules for ambiguous cases and review disagreement.

questions.question: Does token accuracy alone describe entity-span quality?
questions.answer: No. Span boundaries and label correctness matter.

questions.question: Are topic-model groups automatically true classes?
questions.answer: No. They require interpretation and validation.

14.mistake: Changing the annotation unit changes what a reported accuracy denominator means.

14.title: Similarity, retrieval and inference
14.objective: Diagnose a text pair with high overlap but contradictory meaning.
14.idea: Semantic similarity and retrieval seek useful related content, while inference tasks assess relationships such as entailment or contradiction. Translation, summarization and question answering generate outputs that need fidelity checks. Coreference resolution identifies references in context and can fail when entities are ambiguous.
14.example: "The service is available" and "The service is not available" share most words but contradict each other. High lexical overlap does not establish agreement.
14.practice: Write a paraphrase, contradiction and unrelated sentence for one policy statement; define separate labels for similarity and entailment.

questions.question: Does similar wording establish entailment?
questions.answer: No. Negation and other differences can reverse meaning.

questions.question: Can a fluent summary add an unsupported detail?
questions.answer: Yes. Check each important claim against the source.

14.mistake: Retrieval relevance is not the same target as sentence truth or logical support.

14.title: Generation, multilinguality and evaluation
14.objective: Compare a text-generation score with a direct fidelity check.
14.idea: Generated text can be fluent while violating source facts or task constraints. Multilingual behavior depends on language, domain and data coverage. Automatic overlap metrics measure selected properties and should be complemented by relevant human or task checks.
14.example: A summary changes "may close" to "will close". It retains words yet strengthens the claim beyond the source.
14.practice: Evaluate two short summaries for omitted qualifiers, unsupported claims and language-specific errors; define a rubric before choosing the winner.

questions.question: Does high word overlap guarantee factual fidelity?
questions.answer: No. Crucial qualifiers can still change.

questions.question: Can an English-only score establish multilingual performance?
questions.answer: No. Evaluate the relevant languages and user conditions.

14.mistake: A metric should be interpreted according to what it measures, not treated as universal language quality.

15.title: Queries, keys and attention weights
15.objective: Compute a weighted value sum from supplied attention weights.
15.idea: Attention compares queries with keys to choose a weighted combination of values. Scaled dot-product attention divides dot products by the square root of key dimension before softmax. Multiple heads allow different learned projections, while self- and cross-attention use different sources for queries and context.
15.example: Given attention weights [0.25,0.75] and scalar values [2,6], the weighted output is 0.25×2+0.75×6=5. The weights are supplied here rather than claimed as a computed model result.
15.practice: Compute the output for weights [0.6,0.4] and values [1,4], then explain the effect of swapping values while keeping weights fixed.

questions.question: What is the first output?
Must attention weights sum to one under ordinary softmax attention?
questions.answer: Yes, across the permitted key positions for each query.

15.mistake: Attention weights are not automatically a faithful causal explanation of a final prediction.

15.title: Positions, masks and model blocks
15.objective: Diagnose target leakage in a three-position attention mask.
15.idea: Position information distinguishes token order that attention alone may not encode. Causal masks block future positions, while bidirectional attention allows both directions in the supplied input. Residual, feedforward and normalization blocks transform representations with explicit shape and mask requirements.
15.example: For three tokens, a causal allowed-position matrix has rows [1,0,0], [1,1,0], [1,1,1]. Allowing position 3 in row 1 would expose future information.
15.practice: Write the four-token causal matrix and identify which cells must remain blocked when predicting each next token.

questions.question: Can a mask error create training leakage?
questions.answer: Yes. Future targets can become visible.

questions.question: Does positional encoding replace every need for an attention mask?
questions.answer: No. Position and permitted visibility are separate concerns.

15.mistake: Do not infer that every Transformer is a causal decoder; inspect its actual architecture and objective.

15.title: Context, complexity and inference caches
15.objective: Compare attention-pair counts before and after doubling sequence length.
15.idea: Dense attention forms pairwise interactions across sequence positions. Doubling sequence length quadruples the number of position pairs under that simple model. Efficient kernels and key-value caches change execution and memory behavior without removing the need to check actual model and hardware constraints.
15.example: A 4-token sequence has 4×4=16 query-key position pairs, while 8 tokens have 64. This counts pairs, not an exact runtime or memory measurement.
15.practice: Count pairs for lengths 10 and 20, then distinguish a theoretical count from a benchmark including caching and implementation effects.

questions.question: What is the pair-count ratio?
Does a KV cache remove all inference cost?
questions.answer: No. New-token computation and attending to cached context still cost resources.

15.mistake: A complexity expression is not a hardware latency prediction.

15.title: Sparse, long-context and expert designs
15.objective: Compare a sliding-window visibility pattern with full attention.
15.idea: Sparse and sliding-window designs restrict which position pairs interact. Long-context models need evaluation of evidence use, not only a declared input limit. Mixture-of-experts designs route some computation through selected components, and training and inference have different resource profiles.
15.example: A window retaining the two preceding tokens lets position 5 see positions 3,4,5 under an inclusive-self convention. It does not directly see position 1 in that layer.
15.practice: Draw the six-token allowed-position table for this window, then identify which distant facts need another route to influence the final position.

questions.question: Does accepting a long input guarantee using every fact correctly?
questions.answer: No. Evaluate retrieval and reasoning behavior across positions.

questions.question: Does sparse attention use every position pair?
questions.answer: No. Its pattern intentionally excludes some interactions.

15.mistake: A total parameter count does not by itself specify activated computation per token in an expert model.

16.title: Tokens and language-model objectives
16.objective: Compare autoregressive and masked-token prediction on a short sentence.
16.idea: Language models learn patterns over token sequences, and tokens need not coincide with words. An autoregressive objective predicts a next token using preceding context, while masked-language objectives recover hidden tokens from available context. Architecture families and tokenizer choices influence what inputs the model can process, but the family name does not determine factual correctness.
16.example: For "The cat sat", an autoregressive training example can use "The cat" to predict the next token. A masked example can use "The [MASK] sat" to predict the missing token; this is a conceptual trace, not a tokenizer output.
16.practice: Write one next-token and one masked-token training example for a four-word sentence; mark which context each prediction can use.

questions.question: Are tokens always whole words?
questions.answer: No. A tokenizer may produce subword, byte-related or other token units.

questions.question: Does next-token probability represent a fact-checking score?
questions.answer: No. It scores continuations under the model, not verified truth.

16.mistake: A GPT-style or BERT-style label describes a broad family; check the actual model documentation before assuming capabilities.

16.title: Pretraining, context and model structure
16.objective: Diagnose a context-budget failure in a hypothetical model request.
16.idea: Pretraining adjusts parameters using a training objective and dataset. At inference, a context window limits the token sequence the model can use; it is distinct from the stored model parameters. Dense and mixture-of-experts designs distribute computation differently, so parameter count alone does not specify request cost or quality.
16.example: A hypothetical total sequence budget of 100 tokens with 70 input tokens leaves at most 30 for output under that stated accounting rule. Real systems may account for additional token categories, so consult their current specification.
16.practice: Allocate a hypothetical 100-token total budget across instruction, retrieved text and output; show which text you would remove if the input grows by 20.

questions.question: Does a larger parameter count guarantee better task performance?
questions.answer: No. Data, training, inference configuration and the evaluated task also matter.

questions.question: Does adding context update model weights?
questions.answer: No. Ordinary inference conditions on context without retraining weights.

16.mistake: A long context window does not guarantee reliable use of every fact placed in that context.

16.title: Instruction tuning and preferences
16.objective: Compare demonstration-based and preference-based adaptation evidence.
16.idea: Instruction tuning uses examples of desired task behavior. Preference optimization uses comparisons or related preference signals to change output tendencies; different algorithms implement this differently. Better alignment with a preference dataset does not establish that outputs are factual, harmless or suitable for every user.
16.example: A demonstration dataset maps a question to an approved answer. A preference pair ranks a supported concise answer above an unsupported confident answer; that ranking is a training signal, not proof of general truthfulness.
16.practice: Create two synthetic demonstrations and two ranked answer pairs for a policy FAQ; record why the preferred answer is supported and what the dataset cannot establish.

questions.question: Does preference optimization remove the need for evaluation?
questions.answer: No. Evaluate held-out behavior and tradeoffs after adaptation.

questions.question: Is a base model identical to an instruction-tuned model?
questions.answer: No. Post-training can change how it responds to instructions.

16.mistake: A preference label reflects the annotation criteria; it is not automatically an objective truth label.

16.title: Inference, examples and reasoning
16.objective: Compare a zero-shot prompt with a few-shot prompt on held-out inputs.
16.idea: In-context learning supplies examples during inference rather than updating parameters. Additional inference computation may improve some tasks but adds resource use and does not guarantee a correct result. A displayed reasoning narrative is an output to evaluate, not a trustworthy record of every internal operation.
16.example: A prompt containing two date-format examples asks for a third conversion. Success on the third input demonstrates that case only; a separate ambiguous date is needed to test the boundary.
16.practice: Write zero-shot and two-example date-format prompts, reserve three unfamiliar cases and compare outputs using the same acceptance rule.

questions.question: Does few-shot prompting normally retrain weights?
questions.answer: No. The examples condition that inference request.

questions.question: Does a convincing explanation verify the answer?
questions.answer: No. Check the answer against external evidence or a suitable computation.

16.mistake: Do not infer reliable reasoning from fluency or demand hidden internal reasoning as proof; inspect observable results.

16.title: Limitations, benchmarks and model choice
16.objective: Diagnose unsupported claims in a small model comparison.
16.idea: An LLM can generate plausible unsupported content, including invented citations. Benchmark results depend on task coverage, contamination controls and evaluation configuration.
