46.idea: Scientific communication lets others inspect and challenge the reasoning and results. Peer review and conference acceptance provide scrutiny but do not certify that every claim is correct. Ethics, contributor attribution and data permissions apply throughout open collaboration.
46.example: A reproduction cannot run because a dataset version is missing. The handover should identify this gap rather than claim an independently confirmed result.
46.practice: Create a one-page synthetic research report with question, method, actual-versus-proposed results, limitations, artifact versions and contribution credits.

questions.question: Does peer review prove every result?
questions.answer: No. It is a review process with limits.

questions.question: May a failed reproduction be reported as a successful replication?
questions.answer: No. State the actual result and unresolved cause.

46.mistake: A polished presentation cannot substitute for accessible evidence and honest limitations.

47.title: Rule and search project boundaries
47.objective: Implement a bounded rule-based chatbot with a tested fallback.
47.idea: A beginner project should have a small input-output contract before adding a model. Rules and game-search exercises demonstrate decisions without claiming general language understanding. Search depth, state validity and unknown inputs need explicit limits and tests.
47.example: A rule recognizes normalized "hours" and returns a stated schedule; "weather" returns Not found. This is exact-rule behavior, not a trained chatbot.
47.practice: Build the two-input FAQ rule and test case variation, unknown text and empty input; optionally trace one small game move tree without a real game-service integration.

questions.question: Does an exact-match FAQ understand every paraphrase?
questions.answer: No. Test its actual matching behavior.

questions.question: Is a chess move suggestion guaranteed optimal at any depth?
questions.answer: No. Its search and evaluation are bounded.

47.mistake: A successful toy project does not demonstrate mastery of every original project variant listed here.

47.title: Prediction and clustering projects
47.objective: Compare a simple classifier or regressor with an explicit baseline.
47.idea: The listed prediction, segmentation and image tasks require different targets and metrics. Select one bounded project and document the other variants as later work rather than claim they were all built. Data splitting, preprocessing and baseline evaluation are part of the project, not optional polish.
47.example: A 9:1 label dataset gives an always-majority classifier 90% accuracy. Matching it does not establish a useful minority-class detector.
47.practice: Choose one synthetic classification or regression dataset, document labels and split policy, fit a baseline and report an error analysis with an independent changed input.

questions.question: Does 90% accuracy always imply useful prediction?
questions.answer: No. Class balance and error consequences matter.

questions.question: Can one project check complete every variant automatically?
questions.answer: No. Record the exact demonstrated scope.

47.mistake: Keep forecasting temporal and related images grouped; a convenient random split can leak task information.

48.title: Neural and vision project experiments
48.objective: Implement a reproducible neural-project plan with a non-neural baseline.
48.idea: Neural-from-scratch, convolutional, detection and Transformer projects have different compute and prerequisite needs. Keep a small task and a simple baseline before increasing architecture complexity. Fine-tuning a language model is another optional variant, not a required hidden dependency for a small image project.
48.example: A learner trains an image classifier but has not supplied object boxes. The result cannot be claimed as a tested object detector.
48.practice: Choose a small synthetic or authorized image task; specify the target, baseline, grouped split, training budget and a clean-folder reproduction checklist.

questions.question: Does an image-class label test detection boxes?
questions.answer: No. These are different target types.

questions.question: Must a small classifier project include LLM fine-tuning?
questions.answer: No. Choose a bounded variant and state its prerequisites.

48.mistake: A framework tutorial run does not establish independent adaptation or a fair baseline comparison.

48.title: Language, retrieval and time-series variants
48.objective: Compare prerequisites and evidence for retrieval versus forecasting project variants.
48.idea: Text, speech, retrieval and forecasting projects differ in data representation and evaluation. Retrieval needs relevance and source checks, while forecasting needs past-only information and a temporal baseline. Choose one variant and explicitly mark any additional prerequisite topics before beginning.
48.example: A semantic-search project returns a relevant document but generates no summary. That is a valid bounded retrieval scope, not a completed summarization system.
48.practice: Plan one retrieval or forecasting variant with an acceptance rubric, additional prerequisites, negative case and independent change; label unbuilt variants deferred.

questions.question: Can retrieval success prove generated-answer quality?
questions.answer: No. It tests a different stage.

questions.question: Can random splits always validate a time-series project?
questions.answer: No. Preserve the historical information boundary.

48.mistake: Do not present one implemented variant as completion of all listed intermediate projects.

49.title: Assistant contracts and extraction projects
49.objective: Implement a model-independent extraction contract with a deterministic test adapter.
49.idea: Hosted and local assistants need stable input-output boundaries regardless of model choice. Extraction and summarization require structure and source-fidelity checks, while code and voice variants add their own execution or modality constraints. Start offline with a deterministic adapter and label real-model observations separately.
49.example: A mock adapter returns {"city":"Oslo"} for a synthetic request. This tests the application contract but does not establish that a real model extracts cities correctly.
49.practice: Build a mock city-extraction flow with malformed-output, missing-value and unsupported-value tests; describe the separate account, cost and data checks for optional real-model use.

questions.question: Does a passing mock test establish model quality?
questions.answer: No. It checks the fixture and application behavior.

questions.question: Does valid JSON prove correct values?
questions.answer: No. Validate against the input and required semantics.

49.mistake: Do not report real-model latency or cost from a deterministic mock run.

49.title: Document and multimodal RAG variants
49.objective: Diagnose a citation-aware project that retrieves forbidden or stale material.
49.idea: Document, website and multimodal RAG variants add ingestion, retrieval and provenance boundaries. Graph and conversational variants change evidence access and state but retain the same authorization requirements. Complete the relevant retrieval prerequisites before claiming a tested RAG variant.
49.example: A FAQ cites a deleted document still held in its vector index. The answer may sound right but violates the deletion and freshness contract.
49.practice: Plan a synthetic citation-aware FAQ with access-filter, unsupported-question, update and deletion tests; identify additional Topic 18 and 19 work required.

questions.question: Does a source identifier prove source support?
questions.answer: No. Inspect the source content and its relevance.

questions.question: Can conversation memory bypass access checks?
questions.answer: No. Every reused source must remain authorized.

49.mistake: A prototype should state which ingestion formats and retrieval variants were actually tested.

49.title: Domain adaptation project variant
49.objective: Compare prompt-only and adapter-training approaches using held-out evidence.
49.idea: A domain-specific assistant can be changed by prompting, retrieval or parameter adaptation. Fine-tuning requires a justified dataset, baseline and regression evaluation rather than merely a training command. Keep the adaptation variant optional and identify its additional Topic 20 prerequisites.
49.example: A tuned model improves formatting but loses an earlier abstention behavior. The project must report both changes before selecting a release.
49.practice: Write a fine-tuning experiment plan with authorized synthetic examples, a prompt-only baseline, held-out cases, regression tests and a rollback artifact.

questions.question: Does successful training prove useful domain expertise?
questions.answer: No. Evaluate actual task behavior.

questions.question: May held-out examples become tuning examples while retaining the same independent score?
questions.answer: No. Create new evaluation evidence after reuse.

49.mistake: Do not call an assistant domain-accurate based only on fluent domain vocabulary.

50.title: Bounded tools and research workflows
50.objective: Implement a deterministic tool dispatcher that rejects unknown actions.
50.idea: Calculator, lookup, file, SQL and analysis tools expose different data and action surfaces. A dispatcher should validate the tool name, arguments and authorized resource scope before execution. Start with synthetic or read-only fixtures and keep generated instructions separate from policy.
50.example: Allowed tools are add and read_public. A proposal {"tool":"delete_all"} is rejected even if the retrieved text asks for it.
50.practice: Build an offline dispatcher with add and synthetic read_public tools; test unknown tool, wrong argument type and forbidden record ID.

questions.question: Can a retrieved document authorize a new tool?
questions.answer: No. Only trusted application policy can.

questions.question: Does read-only mean free of privacy risk?
questions.answer: No. Reading and exposing unauthorized data can still harm.

50.mistake: A correct final answer does not excuse a forbidden intermediate tool access.

50.title: Interactive actions and concrete approvals
50.objective: Diagnose a changed action proposal after approval.
50.idea: Calendar, email and browser actions can affect external systems and people. Protocol integrations and planner-executor designs do not expand authorization. Bind approval to the concrete destination, content and action, and keep the learning exercise as a mock or paper trace unless actual actions are authorized.
50.example: A reviewer approves mock email draft A to recipient X. Changing to recipient Y requires reconsidering approval before any real send.
50.practice: Create a mock approval record with action, recipient, content hash and expiry policy; test changed recipient and changed content without sending messages.

questions.question: Does approval for draft A automatically cover draft B?
questions.answer: No. Check whether the changed action remains within authorized scope.

questions.question: Does protocol compatibility establish permission?
questions.answer: No. Authorization is separate.

50.mistake: Never use a classroom side-effect example as implicit permission to act on a real account.

50.title: Multi-agent, durable and monitored projects
50.objective: Diagnose a resumed multi-agent task with duplicated side effects.
50.idea: Multi-agent workflows need bounded ownership and explicit handoff evidence. Durable execution requires checkpoints and recovery for uncertain outcomes. Self-checking and monitoring support review but cannot certify the correctness of every action.
50.example: Two workers both believe they own publishing a result. Without single ownership or deduplication, the external action can happen twice.
50.practice: Design a simulated two-worker workflow with one action owner, versioned handoff, iteration budget, checkpoint and independent review checks.

questions.question: Does adding agents guarantee independent evidence?
questions.answer: No. They can share the same assumptions or errors.

questions.question: Can a checkpoint omit operation identity for side effects?
questions.answer: It can make safe recovery ambiguous; preserve enough identity to reconcile.

50.mistake: A self-checking agent remains fallible; verify important results against observable evidence.

51.title: Packaging, identity and serving
51.objective: Implement a deployment handover for a local-only service.
51.idea: Serving and containerization package an inference contract for clients. Authentication, authorization and RAG access remain separate checks around the packaged model. A local deployment can demonstrate reproducibility without claiming public availability, capacity or operational readiness.
51.example: A container returns a valid public FAQ answer on localhost. That does not establish a secure public endpoint, real user authentication or scalable inference.
51.practice: Create a local service handover with exact versions, startup/stop commands, contract tests, identity assumption and forbidden-input cases.

questions.question: Does a container image prove secure deployment?
questions.answer: No. Configuration and surrounding controls matter.

questions.question: Is localhost testing the same as public load testing?
questions.answer: No. Network and workload conditions differ.

51.mistake: Keep the demonstrated environment explicit rather than labeling a local prototype production-ready.

51.title: Release, observability and operating costs
51.objective: Diagnose a release lacking a tested rollback and meaningful metrics.
51.idea: Evaluation pipelines, prompt versions and CI/CD connect changes to acceptance evidence. Tracing, caching, rate limits and cost dashboards need clear measurement scope and privacy boundaries. Monitoring only request success misses quality regressions and may require delayed label or human-review signals.
51.example: A release has lower average latency but more unsupported answers. A rollback rule based only on HTTP 200 responses would miss the quality regression.
51.practice: Write a synthetic release gate with regression, quality, timeout, cost and rollback checks; specify the log fields and retention policy.

questions.question: Does HTTP success establish answer correctness?
questions.answer: No. Task quality needs separate evaluation.

questions.question: Can an untested rollback be claimed reliable?
questions.answer: No. Exercise the intended recovery path.

51.mistake: An operational dashboard should not imply measurements that were never collected.

51.title: Enterprise boundaries and security evidence
51.objective: Diagnose an enterprise assistant with role checks missing from cached responses.
51.idea: Enterprise assistants combine data access, actions and operational responsibilities. Role-based checks must apply through retrieval, caches and tool execution rather than only at the UI. A production-readiness claim requires evidence for the actual organization, threats and operating scope beyond this learning fixture.
51.example: A user without finance access receives an answer cached for a finance user. The UI role picker did not protect the cached data path.
51.practice: Design a synthetic enterprise acceptance matrix covering cross-role reads, tool permissions, deletion, incident owner and recovery; mark every untested deployment assumption.

questions.question: Can a UI role filter enforce backend access?
questions.answer: No. The backend must authorize the actual data and actions.

questions.question: Does passing a small security test prove no vulnerabilities remain?
questions.answer: No. It establishes only the tested cases and properties.

51.mistake: Use production-readiness as an evidence-backed organizational decision, not a label earned by copying a project template.
